summary: Describes how GMPLS Label Switched Paths can be aggregated into a hierarchy to improve scalability. A router can create a TE path and advertise it as a forwarding adjacency, a link that other paths can use. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4206 lets a router advertise an existing traffic-engineered path as a link that other routers can use in their own path calculations. This creates nested paths and can reduce the number of separate paths the network has to manage.

questions: what is lsp hierarchy in gmpls
what is an lsp forwarding adjacency
subtitle: How a GMPLS router advertises one label-switched path as a traffic-engineering link for other paths to use.

tldr.problem: A GMPLS network can contain many label-switched paths. Grouping paths into a hierarchy can improve scalability, but routers need a way to advertise and use those aggregates.
tldr.mechanism: A router creates a traffic-engineered LSP and advertises it as a forwarding adjacency in the same IS-IS or OSPF control-plane instance. Other routers can compute paths over that adjacency and nest their LSPs through it.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4206 defines routing attributes, LSP region boundaries and RSVP-TE and CR-LDP signaling procedures for forwarding adjacencies. It is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 6001 and RFC 6107.

facts.label: Default TE metric
facts.value: max(1, (TE metric of the FA-LSP path) - 1)

today: RFC 4206 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 6001 and RFC 6107. Read those updates together with this document.

sections.title: A Path That Becomes a Link
sections.content:
A Label Switching Router (LSR) can create a Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS) traffic-engineered LSP, then advertise it as a traffic-engineering link in the same IS-IS or OSPF control-plane instance. The advertised link is a forwarding adjacency (FA), and its underlying LSP is the FA-LSP.

Routers flood forwarding-adjacency information like other traffic-engineering links. They can then include those adjacencies in path calculations and establish LSPs over the resulting route. This RFC does not cover an LSP created by one control-plane instance and used as a link by another.
sections.plainLanguage: A router can tell its peers to treat one of its established paths as a link. Other routers can then plan new paths that use that link.

sections.title: Advertising a Forwarding Adjacency
sections.content:
An FA can be numbered or unnumbered. For a numbered IPv4 FA, the originating LSR allocates a /31; the head-end address is the FA-LSP tunnel sender address and the other endpoint address can be inferred. Multiple LSPs between the same endpoints may be advertised separately or combined using link bundling.

A statically provisioned FA gets its attributes from configuration. A dynamically created FA inherits attributes from the LSP that triggered it, and its bandwidth must be at least that LSP's bandwidth. The FA is announced into the same IS-IS or OSPF instance used to create the underlying path.
sections.plainLanguage: The router advertises the path with addressing and traffic details. It can combine several paths into one advertised link, or advertise each path separately.

sections.title: Traffic-Engineering Attributes
sections.content:
The RFC specifies how routing advertisements describe an FA. Its default traffic-engineering metric is max(1, (metric of the FA-LSP path) - 1), which makes the FA attractive when routers compute paths. Its default reservable and unreserved bandwidth is based on the FA-LSP bandwidth.

The FA's switching capability comes from the first link in its path. Its advertised MTU is the minimum along that path for packet-switch capable interfaces. An FA may also advertise the union of the Shared Risk Link Groups (SRLGs) of its underlying links, allowing other routers to consider shared failure risks.
sections.plainLanguage: Routing advertisements give each forwarding adjacency a cost, capacity and switching type. Those details help other routers decide whether the path is suitable for a new connection.

sections.title: Boundaries Between LSP Regions
sections.content:
Interface switching capabilities define LSP regions and help identify where a path crosses from one region to another. The RFC orders the capabilities as PSC-1, PSC-2, PSC-3, PSC-4, TDM, LSC and FSC. For two TDM interfaces, maximum LSP bandwidth also determines their relative order.

A router at a boundary is an edge LSR for that path. Path computation can use the boundaries to restrict which links an LSP traverses, such as limiting a path to links with a specified switching capability.
sections.plainLanguage: Switching capabilities mark the kinds of links a path uses. A change in capability can mark the edge of a region, which helps routers decide where a nested path begins or ends.

sections.title: Signaling LSPs Through an FA
sections.content:
When an LSP is tunneled through an FA-LSP, the head-end treats the FA-LSP tail-end as one IP hop away while processing the explicit route. It subtracts the tunneled LSP's bandwidth from the FA's unreserved bandwidth.

For RSVP-TE, the Path message carries an IF_ID RSVP_HOP object identifying the FA-LSP; the usual Router Alert option and IP-TTL-versus-RSVP-TTL check are not used. For CR-LDP, the Request carries an IF_ID TLV and the head-end creates a targeted LDP session with the tail-end. If no suitable FA-LSP exists, the router can establish and advertise a new one.
sections.plainLanguage: The signaling message identifies the forwarding adjacency so the far endpoint can process the request. If an existing path does not fit, the router can create a new forwarding adjacency for later use.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Using an FA changes the assumption that the data interface and the interface carrying a control message are the same. For RSVP, the control route can change, so security associations may need to identify the sender or receiver by IP address rather than by interface.

The RFC points to RSVP cryptographic authentication and notes that CR-LDP messages use TCP sessions, with TCP MD5 identified as the recommended authentication and integrity mechanism. It also says the security objections to IPsec Authentication Header should be reconsidered for the changed Path-message addressing.
sections.plainLanguage: Control messages may travel over a route different from the data path. The security checks therefore need to identify the relevant endpoint clearly, even when the route changes.
